claims.text: High-energy ball milling under argon followed by vacuum spark plasma sintering produces an ultrafine- or nanocrystalline-grained CoCrFeNiTi microstructure.
The processed microstructure contains an extensive grain-boundary network.
The extensive grain-boundary network promotes grain-boundary-mediated deformation over classical dislocation pile-up strengthening.
Grain-boundary-mediated deformation reduces the alloy's resistance to deformation and causes relatively low hardness and strength.
The starting material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase simple solid-solution state.
The starting material has a nanostructured or ultrafine-grained microstructure resulting from ball milling and rapid sintering.
The high grain-boundary fraction accommodates deformation through grain-boundary sliding or dynamic recovery.
Grain-boundary sliding and rapid recovery reduce dislocation accumulation.
Reduced dislocation accumulation prevents substantial dislocation pile-ups.
Suppression of dislocation accumulation and pile-ups results in lower hardness and strength while maintaining plasticity.
Ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered samples will have lower hardness and yield strength than conventionally processed samples.
Conventionally processed CoCrFeNiTi will generally have coarser grains than material made by the ball-milling and spark-plasma-sintering route.
Conventionally processed, coarser-grained CoCrFeNiTi will exhibit stronger dislocation-based hardening.
In-situ deformation observations of the ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered material will reveal grain-boundary activity rather than dominant dislocation pile-ups.
A conventionally cast or slowly sintered control will have higher hardness and strength than the ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered sample.
Deformation of the conventionally processed control will be dominated by dislocation glide and accumulation.
The proposed mechanism applies under room-temperature loading and typical strain rates used in standard mechanical tests.
Grain-boundary segregation, residual stresses, or undetected minor secondary phases could affect the deformation behavior.
